quote: Meta-analysis of 48 RCTs (6,674 participants) demonstrating lithium reduces completed suicides (OR 0.13) and deaths from any cause (OR 0.38). The strongest evidence for any pharmacological anti-suicide intervention.
problem: The Top-25 summary presents the 2013 meta-analysis as settled proof and calls it the strongest anti-suicide pharmacological evidence. The suicide OR comes from very few events, and the one large RCT designed to test the question, the VA Li+ Plus trial (Katz et al., JAMA Psychiatry 2022; n=519), was stopped for futility with no reduction in suicide-related events (HR 1.10). The summary also uses 'completed suicides'.
whyItMatters: A resident may add lithium to usual care for a recently suicidal patient on the belief that it is proven suicide prevention, and may lean on it in place of means restriction, safety planning and follow-up.
evidence: Cipriani A et al. BMJ 2013;346:f3646. Katz IR et al. JAMA Psychiatry 2022;79(1):24-32 (PMID 34787653): trial stopped for futility; no overall difference in repeated suicide-related events (HR 1.10, 95% CI 0.77-1.55).
correction: Meta-analysis of 48 RCTs (6,674 participants) finding fewer suicides with lithium than placebo (OR 0.13, based on few events) and fewer deaths from any cause (OR 0.38). Still the main pharmacological anti-suicide signal in mood disorders, but read it with the VA Li+ Plus RCT (Katz et al., JAMA Psychiatry 2022), which was stopped for futility after lithium added to usual care did not reduce suicide-related events.
verified: PubMed: Katz 2022 abstract (PMID 34787653) confirmed; Cipriani 2013 figures by recall

quote: CM only efficacious intervention; strong recommendation
problem: The ASAM/AAAP guideline names contingency management as the standard of care, not the only effective intervention. It also recommends CBT and community reinforcement approaches and says pharmacotherapies (e.g., bupropion plus naltrexone for methamphetamine use disorder) may be used off-label. The canon's own #180 (ADAPT-2) reports a positive medication trial, so the summary contradicts itself.
whyItMatters: A resident may withhold evidence-supported psychotherapies or off-label pharmacotherapy from a patient with stimulant use disorder where CM is not available, which is most US settings.
evidence: ASAM/AAAP Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Stimulant Use Disorder, J Addict Med 2024;18(1S Suppl 1):1-56 (PMID 38669101), key takeaways: 'Contingency management represents the current standard of care ... Pharmacotherapies may be utilized off-label to treat StUDs.'
correction: CM is the standard of care and has the strongest evidence; CBT and community reinforcement approach also recommended, and off-label pharmacotherapy (e.g., bupropion + naltrexone for methamphetamine use disorder) may be considered

quote: CAPS-5 d=0.91; 67% no longer met PTSD criteria
problem: The summary gives the phase 3 efficacy result and nothing about what happened next. In August 2024 the FDA issued a complete response letter declining approval of MDMA-assisted therapy, citing concerns about trial design (functional unblinding/expectancy) and data. As of September 2026 it is still not FDA-approved.
whyItMatters: Read on its own, the summary suggests an effective treatment that residents could recommend or refer patients to, when it is unapproved and the evidence behind it was judged insufficient.
evidence: FDA complete response letter to Lykos Therapeutics, Aug 2024 (reported by Psychiatric Times, BioSpace, Science); MAPS statement Aug 2026 describes regulatory 'progress', not approval.
correction: CAPS-5 d=0.91; 67% no longer met PTSD criteria. Not FDA-approved: the FDA declined approval in 2024 (complete response letter) over trial-design and data concerns
verified: WebSearch: FDA CRL 2024 and status through Aug 2026

quote: Established DBT as the first empirically validated treatment for BPD and the model for manualized psychotherapy research.
problem: The 2006 trial did not establish DBT as the first empirically validated BPD treatment. Linehan's 1991 RCT did that, and the 2006 paper's own background describes DBT's efficacy as already 'well-documented'. What the 2006 trial showed was that DBT's benefit is specific to DBT and not simply the effect of expert non-behavioral therapy.
whyItMatters: Residents would misstate the history and the design logic of the trial: it was a dismantling-style control for therapist expertise, not a first demonstration.
evidence: Linehan MM et al. Arch Gen Psychiatry 2006;63(7):757-66 (PMID 16818865), abstract Context/Objective; Linehan MM et al. Arch Gen Psychiatry 1991;48(12):1060-4.
correction: Showed that DBT's benefit is specific to DBT rather than to expert psychotherapy in general, confirming the 1991 Linehan trial that first established DBT as an empirically supported treatment for BPD.

quote: "Clozapine for the Treatment-Refractory Schizophrenic," Arch Gen Psychiatry 1988
problem: The title is misquoted. The paper is 'Clozapine for the treatment-resistant schizophrenic. A double-blind comparison with chlorpromazine.'
whyItMatters: A title search on the misquoted wording fails, and the page tells residents to verify citations against the primary sources.
evidence: Kane J, Honigfeld G, Singer J, Meltzer H. Arch Gen Psychiatry 1988;45(9):789-96 (PMID 3046553).
correction: "Clozapine for the Treatment-Resistant Schizophrenic: A Double-blind Comparison With Chlorpromazine," Arch Gen Psychiatry 1988

quote: with agomelatine, escitalopram, mirtazapine, and venlafaxine among the most efficacious
problem: The list leaves out amitriptyline, which had the largest effect versus placebo in Cipriani 2018 (OR 2.13). It also drops paroxetine and vortioxetine from the paper's head-to-head 'more effective' group.
whyItMatters: Residents would miss the paper's much-taught finding that an older TCA topped the efficacy ranking, which is the reason efficacy has to be weighed against acceptability.
evidence: Cipriani A et al. Lancet 2018;391:1357-66, abstract Findings: ORs from 2.13 (amitriptyline) to 1.37 (reboxetine); head-to-head, agomelatine, amitriptyline, escitalopram, mirtazapine, paroxetine, venlafaxine and vortioxetine more effective.
correction: with amitriptyline showing the largest effect versus placebo and, head-to-head, agomelatine, amitriptyline, escitalopram, mirtazapine, paroxetine, venlafaxine, and vortioxetine more effective than other antidepressants

quote: Emslie et al., "Treatment of Resistant Depression in Adolescents (TORDIA)," AJP 2008–2010
problem: The primary TORDIA report is Brent et al., JAMA 2008. Emslie et al., AJP 2010 is the 24-week follow-up. 'AJP 2008–2010' is not a citable reference.
whyItMatters: The reference sends residents to the wrong primary paper for the trial's main result.
evidence: Brent D et al. JAMA 2008;299(8):901-13; Emslie GJ et al. Am J Psychiatry 2010;167(7):782-91 (the latter appears in this page's reference list).
correction: Brent et al., "Switching to Another SSRI or to Venlafaxine With or Without CBT for Adolescents With SSRI-Resistant Depression (TORDIA)," JAMA 2008 (24-week outcomes: Emslie et al., AJP 2010)
verified: recall; Emslie 2010 reference present in page

quote: "Matching Alcoholism Treatments to Client Heterogeneity," ACER 1997
problem: The Project MATCH posttreatment outcomes paper was published in J Stud Alcohol 1997, not Alcohol Clin Exp Res. ACER carried the 1993 rationale paper (which is in this page's reference list) and the 1998 three-year outcomes.
whyItMatters: A search by journal and year will not find the cited paper.
evidence: Project MATCH Research Group. J Stud Alcohol 1997;58(1):7-29 (PMID 8979210).
correction: "Matching Alcoholism Treatments to Client Heterogeneity," J Stud Alcohol 1997

problem: The two NNTs measure different outcomes. Acamprosate's NNT of 12 is for preventing return to any drinking. Naltrexone's NNT of 12 is for preventing return to heavy drinking; for any drinking its NNT is 20. Side by side, they read as equivalent drugs on the same outcome.
whyItMatters: Residents may quote naltrexone and acamprosate as interchangeable on abstinence, when acamprosate supports abstinence and naltrexone mainly reduces heavy drinking.
evidence: Jonas DE et al. JAMA 2014;311(18):1889-1900, abstract: NNT to prevent return to any drinking 12 (acamprosate) and 20 (naltrexone 50 mg); to prevent return to heavy drinking 12 (naltrexone 50 mg).
correction: Acamprosate NNT=12 to prevent return to any drinking; naltrexone 50 mg NNT=12 to prevent return to heavy drinking (NNT=20 for any drinking)
